title: Imposter syndrome test: do I have impostor feelings? Free quiz — cv.cm
description: Free imposter syndrome test: rate 14 statements about luck, praise and the fear of being found out to get a score from 0 to 56, what it means and how to deal with it. No sign-up; answers stay in your browser.
lede: Do you put your success down to luck and fear that one day everyone will realize you're not that good? Rate 14 statements to see how strongly impostor feelings show up at work or school.
about: Imposter syndrome, also called the impostor phenomenon, is the nagging feeling that you are not as capable as other people think, that your achievements came from luck or charm, and that sooner or later you will be found out. Psychologists Pauline Clance and Suzanne Imes first described it in 1978 among successful women, and it has since been found in people of every gender, age and job, especially after a promotion, a new school or any step up. It is not a mental illness, but it can lead to overwork, anxiety and turning down chances you deserve.

The statements here were written for cv.cm around the common signs of impostor feelings: discounting praise, crediting luck, fear of being exposed, over-preparing and comparing yourself with others. They are not the Clance Impostor Phenomenon Scale or any other published questionnaire, and half of them describe the opposite so that agreeing with everything lands in the middle. The score bands are a rough guide, not research cut-offs.

faq.q: What are the signs of imposter syndrome?
faq.a: Putting success down to luck, brushing off compliments, fearing you'll be exposed as a fraud, over-preparing or working much longer than others, and comparing yourself with people you think are more talented.

faq.q: How is the score worked out?
faq.a: Each statement scores 0 to 4, and half are reversed, so the total runs from 0 to 56. 18 or less is low, 19 to 37 moderate and 38 or more high.

faq.q: Is imposter syndrome a mental illness?
faq.a: No. It is a common pattern of thinking, not a diagnosis. If it comes with constant worry or low mood, though, it is worth talking to a doctor or counselor.

faq.q: How can I overcome imposter syndrome?
faq.a: Keep a record of your wins and the feedback you get, say "thank you" to praise instead of explaining it away, talk to colleagues or friends (many feel the same), and remember that learning on the job is normal, not proof that you don't belong.

items: When I succeed, I often think I just got lucky.
I can accept a compliment without explaining it away.
I worry that people will discover I'm not as capable as they think.
I believe I've earned my place at work or school.
I over-prepare because I'm afraid of being caught out.
When I make a mistake, I see it as a normal part of learning.
I compare myself with others and feel I don't measure up.
I feel comfortable telling people what I've achieved.
I find it hard to take credit for my part in a team's success.
I trust that I can handle a new challenge, even if it's hard at first.
After a promotion or good grade, I feel more pressure than pride.
I rarely worry that people overestimate me.
I hesitate to apply for things unless I meet every requirement.
I believe my skills are the main reason for my results.

low.name: Few impostor feelings (0–18)
low.body: You seem to see your abilities fairly realistically: you can take credit for your work, accept praise and try new things without feeling like a fraud. That confidence makes it easier to grow. Remember that colleagues or friends who seem sure of themselves may still feel like impostors inside; your steadiness can help them.

moderate.name: Moderate impostor feelings (19–37)
moderate.body: Impostor feelings show up for you sometimes, probably after a new step or when you're around people you admire. That's very common. Try writing down three things you did well each week, saying "thank you" when you're praised, and treating mistakes as learning. Talking about it often reveals that others feel the same.

high.name: Strong impostor feelings (38–56)
high.body: You often feel like a fraud, put your success down to luck and fear being found out, even though your results say otherwise. That can be exhausting and hold you back. Keep evidence of your achievements, share how you feel with a mentor or friend, and question the inner voice that says you don't belong. If the worry spills into anxiety or low mood, a counselor can help.
